title: Habits and the general present
intro: Besides `-ýAr`, Turkmen has a second present tense: the general present in `-Ar` (*geler*, *okar*, *işlär*). It steps back from the moment of speaking. It says what is generally so, what someone does as a rule and what will probably happen, and it is how you promise and offer: *Ertir jaň ederin* (I'll call tomorrow), *Çaý içersiňizmi?* (Will you have some tea?). This unit builds it, gives its unusual negative (*gelmerin*, *gelmez*), and spends a whole section on choosing between `-ýAr` and `-Ar`.

blocks.text: Add `-Ar` to the stem: *-ar* after a back vowel, *-er* after a front one. *gel-* → *geler*, *ýaz-* → *ýazar*. Then add the personal endings you know from the present in [A1 unit 6](a1-u06): *-Yn, -sYň, —, -Ys, -sYňYz, -lAr*. With no ending, it is **he**, **she** or **it**: *geler*.

rows.en: he, she or it comes; will come
you come; you'll come (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **After a vowel**, the tense is just *-r*: *oka-* → *okar*, *ýaşa-* → *ýaşar*. And a stem's final *e* becomes *ä*, as in the polite imperative of [A1 unit 12](a1-u12) (*işläň*): *işle-* → *işlär*, *gürle-* → *gürlär*, *diňle-* → *diňlär*.

rows.en: he, she or it reads; will read
you read; you'll read (plural or polite)
he, she or it works; will work
you work; you'll work (plural or polite)

blocks.text: The verbs that change *t* to *d* before `-ýAr` do it here too, because a vowel follows: *gider*, *eder*, *aýdar*, and every verb made with *etmek*: *jaň eder*, *kömek eder*. Other verbs keep their *t*: *ýatar*, *satar*.

items.tk: Men her gün irden çaý içerin.
items.seg: Men her gün irden çaý iç|er|in.

items.en: My grandfather reads the paper every day.
They usually go to bed late.

blocks.title: How geler sounds
blocks.text: In everyday speech the *l* of *geler* often drops, so the word sounds like one long syllable, as if it were `gēr` with a drawn-out *e*. It is always written *geler*.

blocks.title: Two tenses, a few letters apart
blocks.text: *geler* and *gelýär*, *okar* and *okaýar* are different tenses. After a vowel, `-Ar` is only *-r*: *okar*, never `okaar`. And *işlär* has *ä*: *işler* is the plural of *iş*, **jobs**.

The negative is the one irregular part of this tense. In the first and second persons, put `-mAr` between the stem and the ending: *gel-mer-in*, I don't come, I won't come. In the third person it is `-mAz`: *gelmez*, *gelmezler*. Nothing is left of the *-A* of the positive.

blocks.title: *gelmek*: I don't come, I won't come…

you don't come; you won't come

we don't come; we won't come
you don't come; you won't come (plural or polite)
they don't come; they won't come

rows.en: I don't read; I won't read

blocks.text: `-mAr` and `-mAz` follow the stem's last vowel: *-mar*, *-maz* after a back vowel (*okamaryn*, *okamaz*), *-mer*, *-mez* after a front one (*içmerin*, *içmez*). A stem's *e* stays *e* before them: *işlemerin*, *işlemez*. With *olar*, *gelmez* on its own is also used: *Olar gelmez*.

**Questions** work as in the `-ýAr` present: `-mY` after the ending, all one word. *Gelersiňmi?* Will you come? *Ol gelermi?* Will he come? With *sen* and *siz* you will also see the particle before the ending: *gelermisiň?*, *gelermiň?*, *gelermisiňiz?* All are right; this course writes *gelersiňmi?* and *gelersiňizmi?*

rows.en: Will he, she or it come?
Won't he, she or it come?

blocks.title: Where you'll meet it
blocks.text: In writing, the negative of `-Ar` is less common than the positive. You will meet it in refusals and predictions (*Men gitmerin*, I won't go; *Ol gelmez*, he won't come) and in sayings: *Mundan hiç zat çykmaz*, nothing will come of this.

blocks.title: gelmez is not gelmeýär
blocks.text: *Ol gelmeýär* is **he isn't coming**; *Ol gelmez* is **he won't come** or **he never comes**. Don't mix the two: `gelmeýer` and `gelmezýär` are not words. And **he** or **she** takes no ending after *-mAz*: *gelmez*.

`-ýAr` stays close to now: what is happening, and what really goes on in your life these days. `-Ar` steps back. Grammars of Turkmen call it the indefinite future, and that name fits most of its uses: it says what is likely, what you are willing to do, and what is so in general.

items: **What will probably happen**: *Belki ertir ýagyş ýagar*, maybe it will rain tomorrow; *Elbetde, ol geler*, of course she'll come.
**Promises, and decisions made on the spot**: *Bolýar, men ertir jaň ederin*, OK, I'll call tomorrow; *Men saňa kömek ederin*, I'll help you.
**Offers and polite questions**: *Çaý içersiňizmi?*, will you have some tea? *Sen hem gelersiňmi?*, will you come too?
**What is always so**, and what people and things are like: *Gyşda gar ýagar*, it snows in winter; *Gowy dost kyn günde kömek eder*, a good friend helps on a hard day.
**Habits, as what someone does as a rule**: *Atam her gün ir turar*, my grandfather gets up early every day: that's what he does.

blocks.text: It is also how people part until the next meeting: *Ertir duşuşarys!*, see you tomorrow, literally **we'll meet tomorrow**. And plans often come with *nesip bolsa*, **God willing**: *Indiki ýyl Mara bararyn, nesip bolsa*, next year I'll go to Mary, God willing.

items.en: In winter it snows in Dashoguz.
My grandfather gets up early every day.

blocks.text: These words usually come after the subject, before the rest of the sentence: *Men köplenç çaý içerin*, I often drink tea. *Hiç haçan* needs a negative verb: *Men hiç haçan et iýmerin*, I never eat meat. They go with `-ýAr` just as well: *Men köplenç çaý içýärin*.

blocks.title: nesip bolsa
blocks.text: Turkmen speakers often add *nesip bolsa* when they talk about the future: *Ertir gelerin, nesip bolsa*. It means roughly **if it is meant to be**, **God willing**. Its grammar comes later in the course; for now, use it as a set phrase.
Both tenses can translate an English simple present, and both can talk about the future, so the choice is about how you see the action. A rule of thumb:

items: `-ýAr`: what is happening now, what really happens in your life these days, and fixed plans. For routines it is the everyday choice, and never wrong.
`-Ar`: what is generally so or typical, what will probably happen, and what you promise, offer or are willing to do.

blocks.text: Compare the pairs below. In each pair, the first sentence has `-ýAr` and the second `-Ar`.

items.note: what I do, as a rule

items.en: He doesn't smoke. He isn't smoking.
He doesn't smoke. He'd never smoke.
Are you drinking tea? Do you drink tea?
items.note: a question about what you do

blocks.text: **-jAk or -Ar for will?** `-jAk` ([A2 unit 3](a2-u03)) is the future you have decided on or are sure of; `-Ar` is likelier, softer, or a promise made now. *Men ertir geljek*, I'll come tomorrow: that's settled. *Men ertir gelerin*, I'll come tomorrow: I expect to, I promise.

blocks.title: English draws similar lines
blocks.text: English also separates **I'm calling him tomorrow** (a plan) from **I'll call you** (a promise), and **it's snowing** from **it snows in winter**. Where English uses **will** for a promise or a guess, Turkmen often uses `-Ar`.

blocks.title: When in doubt
blocks.text: For something you do regularly, `-ýAr` is always safe: *Men her gün işe gidýärin*. Keep `-Ar` for promises, offers, guesses and what is always so. And never use it for what is happening right now: for **I'm drinking tea now**, say *Häzir çaý içýärin*, not `Häzir çaý içerin`.

summary: The general present is stem + `-Ar`, or *-r* after a vowel, + the endings *-Yn, -sYň, —, -Ys, -sYňYz, -lAr*: *gelerin, okar, işlärsiň*.
A stem's *e* becomes *ä* before *-r* (*işlär*), and *t* becomes *d* in *gider, eder, aýdar*.
Negative: `-mAr` in the first and second persons, `-mAz` in the third: *gelmerin, gelmersiň, gelmez, gelmezler*.
`-Ar` is for what will probably happen, promises, offers, what is always so, and habits seen as typical.
For what is happening now, for fixed plans and for everyday routines, `-ýAr` is the default.
